statement: Research I designates §9 (determinism and reproducibility) as the section carrying the affirmative case for Entrybound.

The SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH spec mandates clamping, not setting: embedded current timestamps use the variable, and non-current embedded timestamps must be no later than it, so genuinely older timestamps legitimately survive.

No archiver appears in the Reproducible Builds project's table of ~25 SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH-supporting tools (compilers, doc generators, package builders only); archive determinism is achieved via explicit flags or post-hoc mutation, never ambient convention.
research_needed: Re-check the current Reproducible Builds tool table before citing externally.

statement: gzip uses SOURCE_DATE_EPOCH only to disable IBM Z hardware DEFLATE (output may not be reproducible); it does not affect the header MTIME field, which requires -n.
Readdir ordering is a non-determinism source; GNU tar >=1.28 --sort=name fixes it but is locale-sensitive, hence a C-locale requirement.
mtime/atime/ctime, uid/gid and their name strings, and permission bits/umask are live archive non-determinism sources; reprotest varies umask by default.
PAX extended headers embed the process PID when POSIXLY_CORRECT is set, because GNU tar's default extended-header name template contains %p.
gzip header FNAME, MTIME and OS bytes vary output; CPython delegating gzip.compress() to zlib.compress() changed the OS byte and caused reproducible-build failures.

zstd output depends on threading: different job sizes give non-identical frames, --single-thread differs from -T1, --adapt is not reproducible, so -T0 builds differ across machines with different core counts.
research_needed: Measure zstd frame byte identity across worker counts, job sizes and zstd library versions for the Rust binding Entrybound uses.
decision_needed: Must zstd worker count and job size be fixed, or recorded as part of container identity?

statement: ZIP's DOS local-time timestamps are listed as a source of non-determinism.

zlib-ng output bytes are confirmed to differ from zlib: Fedora's accepted change warns checksum-comparing tests may fail; .NET's zlib-ng migration used a size-tolerance criterion; zlib-ng's README claims drop-in but is silent on byte identity.
Whether Chromium's zlib fork produces bytes different from upstream zlib is unverified; no primary source was reached and it must not be asserted.
research_needed: Differential DEFLATE output test: Chromium zlib vs upstream zlib on a fixed corpus and levels.

statement: Neither the zlib manual nor FAQ states that compressed output is stable across zlib versions or platforms (absence verified); the absence of a promise is the operative fact.
Hardware-accelerated DEFLATE is confirmed non-reproducible (gzip disables IBM Z DFLTCC for reproducibility).
strip-nondeterminism is a Perl tool with twelve format handlers, wired into debhelper so it runs on every Debian package build.
strip-nondeterminism's gzip handler rewrites the header, sets/clamps MTIME and drops FNAME, but deliberately preserves XFL and OS bytes — the exact gap that broke CPython.
strip-nondeterminism's ar handler zeroes mtime/uid/gid and collapses modes to 755 or 644, because binutils defaulted to non-deterministic archives.

strip-nondeterminism's zip handler sorts members and canonicalizes DOS timestamps against SAFE_EPOCH = 315576060 (1980-01-01T12:01:00Z), twelve hours past the DOS epoch so no timezone rendering falls below the floor.
decision_needed: Should Entrybound's ZIP export use a timezone-safe DOS timestamp floor such as SAFE_EPOCH for pre-1980 or canonical times?

statement: The zip handler also rewrites the 0x5455 extended timestamp, canonicalizes the 0x000a NTFS field, and zeroes uid/gid in the 0x7875 Info-ZIP Unix extra field, which silently carries ownership most tools never surface.

strip-nondeterminism's jar handler refuses signed JARs (modification breaks signatures), forces META-INF/ ordering, strips Bnd-LastModified and Built-By, and decrements .clj timestamps so they stay older than corresponding .class files.

A metadata normalization policy cannot be a constant function; it must at minimum be order-preserving, since a flat canonical time is deterministic but semantically wrong for consumers depending on relative timestamp ordering.
refines_or_supersedes: Generalization deferred in R1 §21 item 13 L1130
evidence_in_source: inference [INFERENCE] from the single jar.pm .clj case
research_needed: Survey consumers that depend on relative mtime ordering (make, JVM/Clojure, Python bytecode caches) to derive a general rule.
decision_needed: What exact order-preserving time normalization rule does the canonical profile apply?

statement: Fedora reimplemented strip-nondeterminism in Rust as add-determinism.
research_needed: Study add-determinism handlers as Rust prior art for canonicalization of legacy exports.

statement: diffoscope is the diagnostic counterpart to normalization: it recursively unpacks archives to explain a delta rather than merely detect it.

disorderfs randomizes readdir order but recommends --sort-dirents over shuffling so differences are reproducible; reprotest varies fourteen axes, five mapping directly to archive metadata (fileordering, user_group, umask, timezone, locales).
research_needed: Adopt reprotest/disorderfs variation axes in Entrybound's determinism test harness.

statement: Reproducibility status: Debian forky/amd64 94.9% of 39,034 and unstable 94.2% of 41,134 (2026-08-29); Reproducible Central 72.4% (6,270/8,660) with 108 projects at none; F-Droid 83% rebuild success, 94% of those bitwise.
Nix/nixpkgs 'up to 93% in 2024' is cited secondhand; Arch, openSUSE and Fedora reproducibility figures are unverified (dashboards machine-unreadable or no published figure).
research_needed: Obtain primary reproducibility figures from Nix, Arch, openSUSE and Fedora.

statement: No published layer-attributed reproducible-build failure taxonomy exists for any ecosystem (searched, none found).

Debian issue-catalogue proxy: compiler/build-path capture dominates (gcc build path 1,841 packages; cmake rpath 437) while pure archive-layer issues are small (random tarball order 18; random static-library order 38).

Because dh_strip_nondeterminism runs on every Debian build, archive defects are masked not absent; the share of non-determinism the archive layer would cause without universal post-processing is unmeasured.
refines_or_supersedes: Restated as R1 §19 Q1 L1055
research_needed: Rebuild a Debian package sample with dh_strip_nondeterminism disabled and attribute failures by layer.
decision_needed: Is archive-layer non-determinism large enough to justify determinism as the primary product thesis?

statement: Research I cross-references its open research questions as '§18', but they are numbered §19 (§18 is the opportunity assessment).
evidence_in_source: internal cross-reference comparison (auditor observation within source)

statement: NAR grammar is length-prefixed with 8-byte alignment; directory entries MUST be ordered by name; three node types (file = bytes plus one executable boolean, directory, symlink); hard links, permissions, timestamps and other metadata are not encoded.
Lesson from NAR: length-prefixed fixed-alignment framing removes all encoder discretion, because there is no 'extra field' to disagree about.
research_needed: Canonicality check of Entrybound's own encodings: prove or fuzz that each logical value has exactly one accepted byte serialization.

statement: Lessons from NAR: the permission model can be one bit rather than twelve, and ordering belongs as a MUST in the grammar rather than a flag.
Lesson from NAR: not modelling hard links means deduplication ambiguity cannot arise.
Lesson from NAR: keeping compression outside the format means codec drift cannot affect identity.

Go module zips are constrained: every path prefixed <module>@<version>/, no two paths equal under Unicode case-folding, empty directories/permissions/timestamps ignored, no symlinks or irregular files, 500 MiB caps.
Go's h1: module hash is computed as if by sha256sum over sorted file list then sha256sum; only file names and contents count — zip encoding, compression method, mtimes and other metadata are ignored.

Do not make archive bytes the identity: make a canonical manifest the identity and let the archive be a transport whose bytes may vary — called the single most transferable design lesson in the report.
evidence_in_source: inference [INFERENCE] from Go module zip and NAR

statement: Manifest identity immunizes against every §9.2 non-determinism source including codec drift, at the cost of not being able to verify an archive without decoding it.
research_needed: Quantify verify-by-decode cost versus container-byte hash verification on large archives.
decision_needed: Should verification without decoding be supported via a container-level hash in addition to manifest identity?

statement: OCI layer digests are over compressed bytes, so the exact tar stream must be recoverable; tar-split stores raw header bytes and offsets at ~0.06 kB/file to reassemble byte-identical archives.
tar-split is the price of content-addressing a non-canonical container: a side channel recording the encoder's arbitrary choices must be shipped.

IPFS UnixFS content-addresses without mandated canonical encoding: chunker, chunk size, DAG layout and optional mode/mtime all change the root CID; the spec notes including mode causes unnecessary deduplication failures.
research_needed: Verify Entrybound identity roots are invariant under chunker/CDC parameter changes and optional metadata inclusion.

statement: Unconditional tier: given identical file contents, names and a declared metadata policy, the canonical logical serialization (NAR-equivalent layer) is byte-identical — testable and stable forever.
research_needed: Cross-platform, cross-version determinism test suite over the canonical serialization.
decision_needed: How is 'stable forever' reconciled with evolving serialization (versioned identity profiles)?

statement: Version-scoped tier: identical container bytes only for a pinned library version, format, codec and codec parameters, including thread count and job size since zstd makes them part of output identity.
research_needed: Measure container byte identity across OS/CPU architectures with all parameters pinned.

statement: Byte identity of compressed output across codec versions or backends is impossible to promise: no underlying compressor promises it (zlib silent, zlib-ng may break checksum tests, hardware DEFLATE non-reproducible).

Expose two hashes: a content hash over the canonical manifest stable across all backends and versions, and an optional container hash over emitted bytes valid only within a declared codec triple recorded as recoverable metadata.
decision_needed: Which exact fields constitute the recorded codec identity for container-hash validity?

statement: The container-identity pin set is stated inconsistently: library version+format+codec+parameters incl threads/job size (L674); a 'codec triple' (L677); (profile, format, codec, codec parameters) without library version (§14.4c); (format, metadata policy, codec, codec parameters) (§1 L68).
refines_or_supersedes: Internal tension among R1 §1 L68, §9.6 L674/L677, §14 item 4(c) L886, §21 item 24 L1147
evidence_in_source: internal cross-reference comparison (auditor observation within source)
decision_needed: Does the container-byte identity pin tuple include library/planner version, profile, metadata policy, thread count and job size?

statement: Determinism conflicts with fidelity: it requires discarding uid/gid, times and most permission bits that backup and packaging need; practical resolutions are all declared lossy policies (NAR/Git one exec bit, 755/644 collapse, opt-in portable tar, clamping).
decision_needed: How do identity profiles separate metadata that participates in identity from metadata that is carried but excluded?

statement: Signed containers cannot be normalized at all; normalization must always precede signing.
evidence_in_source: cited facts plus inference [FACT + INFERENCE] (jar.pm refusal)

statement: google/safearchive is a drop-in for Go archive/tar and zip with modular checks, but hardening is disabled by default for backward compatibility; it still took CVE-2024-10389, has negligible adoption and is not an officially supported Google product.

hashicorp/go-extract supports 12 formats with the only sane numeric extraction defaults found (100k files, 1 GB, 60 s), but is extraction-only and a vendor-internal tool never positioned as an ecosystem library.

Go os.Root (kernel containment) and Python PEP 706 filters put zip-slip protection at the correct language layer, absorbing the safety wedge into stdlibs — a threat to the thesis rather than a partial solution.
Docker chrootarchive uses a kernel boundary and is correct by construction, but is container-layer specific, Linux-privilege dependent, and now deprecated into moby/go-archive.
yauzl reads ZIP only via the central directory and deliberately refuses to grow — the best-argued scope refusal in the category.
archiver, yazl and zip-stream provide real streaming ZIP creation but are create-only: no extraction, no safety, no determinism.
unzipper (Open.url/Open.s3) and ripunzip use HTTP range requests into a ZIP central directory; ripunzip is ZIP-only, extract-only, and slower than baseline on slow disks.
Browser/edge ZIP libraries are format-locked: zip.js is the most complete single-format library found; client-zip (2.6 kB) explicitly excludes compression, extraction and encryption; fflate likewise.
strip-nondeterminism and add-determinism are post-processing hacks born because no archive library offers determinism as an API; their existence is called the strongest argument for the thesis.
research_needed: Interview reproducible-builds practitioners on whether post-processing is adequate (see §12.1 claim 1).

statement: Per-ecosystem canonicalization (go mod zip, pacote constants, pypa/wheel, pkg_tar, Homebrew gzip wrapper) each solves determinism completely in its domain; described as eight ecosystems, eight reimplementations, though only five are named here.
evidence_in_source: primary citation [FACT] for named items; count of eight not enumerated
research_needed: Enumerate and cite all eight claimed per-ecosystem determinism reimplementations.

statement: tar-split provides bit-exact tar reassembly (~0.06 kB/file), is load-bearing for Docker/OCI yet almost unknown; it is a side channel, not a fix.
ratarmount, indexed_gzip and zran retrofit random access into tar.gz with a SQLite index (150 GB / 2M files remounting in under 1 ms), but are read-only and FUSE-shaped.

The zstd seekable format has sat in contrib/ at spec v0.1.0 since 2017; eStargz (CNCF sub-project integrated into BuildKit, Kaniko, nerdctl) succeeded precisely by remaining readable by unaware runtimes.
Codec-speed projects (libdeflate, zlib-ng, zlib-rs, klauspost/compress, pigz/pzstd) deliver real measured gains only at the codec layer; libdeflate's refusal of streaming shows the ceiling.
Rust async archive support exists only via forks (async-compression, astral-tokio-tar, astral_async_zip); the forks are the wrapper libraries, with a five-generation lineage and one shared CVE.

PNA (portable-network-archive): Rust, PNG-chunk-inspired, zstd/xz/zlib, AES-256, xattrs and ACLs, uniquely explicit determinism claims; 18 stars; later called technically the most thoughtful design surveyed.
research_needed: Direct review of the PNA specification as prior art for native container, determinism and encryption design.

statement: Jubako/arx is a generic container meta-format claiming 215% faster extraction than tar and ~54,000% faster mounting; 164 stars; the benchmark claims are reported, not reproduced.
research_needed: Reproduce Jubako/arx benchmark claims before using them comparatively.

statement: DwarFS (2.6k stars) is genuinely excellent for redundant corpora but is a read-only filesystem image, not an interchange format.
Alpine apk-tools 3.x shipped in Alpine 3.23.0 (Dec 2025) retaining v2 index/package compatibility; the tar-abandoning ADB format is not the default and its design is unverified.
refines_or_supersedes: Restated as R1 §19 Q5 L1059
research_needed: Read apk-tools source to document ADB design, status and rationale.

statement: Successful 'new formats' are those that refused to be new formats (eStargz pushable to standard registries, runnable on agnostic runtimes), while PNA, the only determinism-focused design, has 18 stars; this should discipline any format ambition.
decision_needed: Given this finding, what compatibility bridge (legacy export, dual publishing) justifies a native Entrybound container?

statement: An archive format's value is entirely network effect: an archive only your tool opens is a liability at CI caches, registries, curl|tar pipelines, OS file managers, security scanners and forensic tools; tar-split shows a shim was cheaper than changing format.
research_needed: Evidence on adoption of native formats with and without legacy export paths.
decision_needed: How will native archives interoperate with scanners, registries and file managers that cannot open them?

statement: No comprehensive successor exists, but the thesis is narrower than it looks and two of its four pillars are being eroded by other actors.

libarchive: breadth, near-universal adoption, ARCHIVE_EXTRACT_SECURE_* as reference safety design; but no determinism API, not thread-aware, 59 CVEs, 501 open issues, 15% fuzz coverage for nine years, secure flags off by default, bindings exposing different subsets.

mholt/archives has the cleanest unified API with context.Context cancellation but is Go-only, read-only for 7z and RAR, non-seekable, silent on determinism, and leaves extraction safety to the caller.

Commons Compress has JVM breadth and the most honest limitations page (a catalogue of facade gaps); SharpCompress best articulates the seekability tradeoff (forward-only Readers vs random-access Archives) but is .NET-locked.
ouch is CLI-only with no documented library surface; zip.js and zip2 are excellent single-format libraries; eStargz and ratarmount are domain-specific retrofits.

Nothing occupies the intersection of create/inspect/extract/stream/random-access/determinism/safety/breadth; determinism is the most defensible gap — four ecosystems, four workarounds, zero libraries offering the API call.

Astral and Chainguard funded codecs (libzstd-rs, zlib-rs), not containers; Astral forked a crate and patched two safety behaviors; Microsoft forked libarchive for Windows 11. Unserved gap, or sophisticated organizations concluding a comprehensive archive library isn't worth building?
research_needed: Interview these organizations or comparable adopters on why container-layer work was not funded or built.
decision_needed: Is a container-layer product worth building given vendors' revealed preferences?

statement: Adjacent displacements: ripgrep ~8.9x plus gitignore-awareness and VS Code bundling; uv 10-100x as a pip drop-in with a funded vendor; zlib-ng ~4x and zlib-rs adopted invisibly (Firefox 151.0, 30M downloads); bzip2's Rust backend needing zero user action.

Successful displacements meet at least three of four conditions: a large multiple on one measurable axis; drop-in compatibility at the boundary; a distribution wedge inside something already installed; sustained institutional funding.
research_needed: Test the four-condition model against failed displacement attempts, not only successes.

statement: Entrybound has no available 10x axis: codec performance, parallel extraction and random access are taken; what remains (safety, determinism, ergonomics, cross-format uniformity) are correctness properties, and correctness does not benchmark.
research_needed: Benchmark whether planner-driven compression/dedup yields a measurable multiple versus incumbents, which would contradict this finding.
decision_needed: Does Entrybound claim any measurable superiority axis, and is that claim evidenced?

statement: Because condition (1) is unavailable and (2) exists only for conformant tar/ZIP emitters, conditions (3) and (4) are the whole strategy; the distribution wedge is a technical requirement that must shape the design from day one.
decision_needed: What concrete distribution wedge (host tool, bundling, CLI) shapes the v1 design?

statement: API migration friction is high: Python, Go, Java and .NET incumbents are zero-cost stdlibs (.NET already traversal-safe for tar and ZIP), Node's are lockfile-frozen transitive deps; Rust is the only ecosystem where new dependencies are normal and incumbents weak.

research_needed: Measure strict-mode rejection rate over a real-world archive corpus.

Offer a CLI accepting common GNU tar and Info-ZIP flags plus a --canonical/--profile flag emitting reproducible output without the seven-flag incantation — a cheap distribution wedge requiring no library adoption (ouch and bsdtar as precedents).

statement: The falsification case is stated at full strength and evidence-anchored; claims a research pass could not source were dropped rather than asserted.

The pain is historical: Python 3.14 defaults to the data filter, Go 1.24/1.25 ship os.Root, .NET throws on escapes since .NET 7, node-tar safe since 2021, Node core ZIP at v26.8.0; the unsafe remainder is on old runtimes whose teams rarely add dependencies.
research_needed: Telemetry on runtime versions in production archive-handling code.

statement: The comprehensive successor already exists: libarchive (22 years; macOS, FreeBSD, NetBSD, Windows, CMake, pacman) already has secure-extraction flags; fixing their off-by-default state is a thirty-line wrapper — a weekend, not a product.

Format semantics resist unification: Commons Compress's streaming ZIP reader may return false contents; yauzl calls streaming unzip dishonest or nonconformant; ZipDiff finds no de facto ZIP standard, so a portable deterministic facade over ZIP reading is unshippable.

Safe defaults break real workloads: Go abandoned safe-by-default (absolute paths in Docker images); jdk.zipfs refuses to open archives with '..'; Python says filters don't prevent DoS; every safe library ships an escape hatch that predictably gets pasted everywhere.
research_needed: Usability/adoption study of how often capability grants or escape hatches are used in practice.

statement: That ZIP strictness rejects real APKs and self-extracting archives at scale is unverified and must not be used until measured; only the Gradle issue-tracker case (UnZip CVE-2019-13232 overlap check rejecting jars) is attested.
research_needed: Measure strict ZIP rejection on APK and SFX corpora.

statement: Archive libraries are too low-level and sticky: a successor must beat zero dependencies; jszip (42.8M weekly, no release since 2022) and extract-zip (26.3M, since 2020) persist; being better doesn't propagate up dependency graphs; archive code is written once.

Multi-language is a trap: FFI means eighteen triples per ecosystem and a WASM target lacking the headline feature; independent implementations diverge (four forks shared CVE-2025-62518; ZipDiff across 50 parsers); 'same semantics everywhere' becomes a false security property.
research_needed: Define differential-testing obligations for any independent or minimal reader.

statement: Six months is fantasy: libarchive has 7,965 commits, 501 open issues, 78 open PRs; one Python default took a PEP and three releases; the zip crate still took a CVSS 7.3 symlink flaw; six months yields a demo; credible-for-untrusted-input is three to five years.

Adding a fourth-generation archive library to the graveyard (mholt/archiver archived, tokio-tar abandoned with live CVE, Info-ZIP static since 2009, sevenz-rust dead, xz-utils maintainer-exhaustion attack) increases ecosystem risk unless year-3 maintenance is funded and named.

Model B (capability-typed): extraction requires a containment handle; each dangerous operation is a named, individually granted, auditable capability; tar dialects are types (.NET V7TarEntry/PaxTarEntry/GnuTarEntry) so fidelity is compile-time. Verdict: right internal architecture, poor headline.

statement: Pain severity scored 6: severe or catastrophic in niches (untrusted extraction, reproducible builds, container layers), mild to invisible in median use where the stdlib works.

Pain recurrence scored 9: continuous 2007-2026; Python's filters bypassed at least 8 times since 2024; decompress's patch bypassed and still unfixed; the same defect independently rediscovered in six ecosystems.
Fragmentation scored 8: eight independent determinism reimplementations, a five-generation async fork lineage, facades covering different subsets, per-ecosystem safe-extraction wrappers.
Successor gap scored 7: libarchive owns breadth, runtimes are taking safety, codecs are taken; the genuinely unoccupied ground is determinism plus conformance.

Migration feasibility scored 4: incumbent free, pre-installed, mostly uncounted; Go's stdlib beats the best facade ~124:1 on public importers; archive code written once; lockfile inertia keeps 4-6-year-stale packages at tens of millions of weekly downloads.
Technical feasibility scored 6: core well understood and codec layer solved; the long tail — dialects, encodings, sparse, platform semantics, parser-ambiguity strictness — is where the years go.
Six-month v1 feasibility scored 3 as briefed and 5 under the §16 revised scope.
Multilingual feasibility scored 3: eighteen-triple FFI matrices per ecosystem, a WASM target lacking the headline feature, and demonstrated semantic drift between forks of the same code.
Messaging must be disciplined: 'deterministic, bounded, capability-gated archives' is crisp and defensible (score 6), whereas 'safe archive library' is not and is what the market will hear otherwise.
Likelihood of category recognition scored 4: no 10x axis, correctness does not benchmark, and every adjacent displacement needed a distribution wedge or vendor, neither currently in hand.

Verdict GO WITH REVISED SCOPE (mean 5.9): drop multi-language, unified facade and safety-as-headline; keep a deterministic, capability-gated, containment-based single-language engine emitting conformant tar and ZIP, with a public conformance corpus and a CLI wedge.
